posts.body_html:
It's been sort of a rough start for the sphagnum this year. By this time last year, I think all of the trays were full and there was about an inch or two of growth, but this year things are a lot slower for whatever reason....probably because these were left in full sun all summer long in 2016, which really set everything back quite a bit because it was just too hot. The starting material had already lost momentum and was under stress, and it took a really long time to recover and start growing again. I might leave these in the same spot but cover them with 75% shade cloth once day temps go above 80F, see if that works. Seems that's the ultimate solution for keeping cool growing plants happy during our warm summers: shade.

A few trays still haven't been fully "colonized" and I'm really hoping it fills in cuz this harvest will be used to grow the ever increasing collection of disas. Photos taken 4/4/17:

Nov 20, 2015 16:17:38 GMT -5 meizzwang said:
After discussing the topic of Sphagnum moss in another thread, I figured I'd post a little something about growing this wonderful moss. This outstanding carnivorous plant companion grows in many carnivorous plant habitats across the planet, and there are various species within the genus Sphagnum. It's also an incredible medium for many carnivorous plants, orchids, epiphytes, etc.

I used to buy bales of dried Sphagnum moss every year to repot my Disa orchids (south african terrestrial orchid), but it's becoming more and more difficult to source good quality moss these days. When I did get these bales, grasses and all sorts of other crap came with it. What I've learned is this moss is actually a renewable resource, yet it is harvested commercially from the wild. Anytime you buy this moss, chances are it was from the wild.

My hope is that this post will spark some of you to consider growing it instead of having it harvested from the wild. I've heard from many friends that they dream of becoming a sphagnum farmer, and let me tell you this much: if you become one and are successful, you'll go down in the history books as being the first to pioneer it! No doubt, the methods below can be applied to a commercial operation, and there is no such operation in existence as of today (11/20/15).

Quality bales of Sphagnum go for more than $100 and have to be shipped half way across the globe to get to California (where I live), so I figured, what the heck, let me see if I can grow this stuff. It was shocking to see how big of a yield you can get from growing your own moss. Within a year, out of seven 10x20 trays, I harvested more than a wheel barrel full (more than a bale) worth of moss! The crazy thing is, it doesn't even look like that much until you actually harvest it.

How do you grow Sphagnum moss? As mentioned earlier, I grow them in 10x20 trays. The trays are 90% filled with old, dead sphagnum moss (or you could fill it with peat moss) and then every fall/early winter, with scissors, I cut the active growth points off my "mother moss plants" and place it in the trays. It's kept very water-logged, and I fertilize with maxsea 1-2x per month. Use slightly lower concentrations as you would for filling up pitchers of Sarracenia. This moss likes as much light as possible, but it also wants to be kept cool.

During the winter, the trays of moss are kept in full sun when it's nice and cold, and once the day temperatures get above 78F, they get morning sun/afternoon shade. I rarely have to water them during the winter, but during the summer, they get overhead watered with low TDS water daily.

Here's a photo of some Sphagnum moss, there are 7 trays total, and this is after a year's worth of growth:


Okay, here comes the shocker. Would you have guessed that those 7 small trays of moss yielded more than a Wheel Barrel full?! I have more harvested that isn't pictured below. Imagine if you had an acre of this moss, and you harvested it annually... Unlike much of the wild stuff, this is free of weeds, sticks, and other crap. I could barely believe my eyes after harvesting this stuff, there was so much of it:



The tops were cut off and placed right back into the original trays. I actually had enough "tops" to plant perhaps 40-50 trays, but space is an issue, so I went for 8 trays this time. In a year, this will look just like the first picture in this thread:



I hope everyone goes out and does this so we place less pressure on wild Sphagnum bogs. It takes up relatively little space, and produces an outstanding yield every year. IF you grow 20-30 trays of this stuff every year, you'll have enough moss to grow a commercial quantity of orchids, epiphytes, carnivorous plants, etc.






Top pics looks like broccoli

www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3886977/#pone.0079991-Rudolph1
Sphagnum Mosses - Masters of Efficient N-Uptake while Avoiding Intoxication

Great article denoting what is likely going on in your grow; buildup of nitrogen is shown to decrease biomass produced. maybe slow your fertilizing roll to bring the levels back down. Then again, it might just be beneficial to decrease ferts post-harvesting or pre- and see if either affects your overall growth rate.

Cheers and thanks for the multi-year grow log!

great input! Yes, if you look at Sarracenia as an analogy, when the soil gets too loaded with nutrients, this leads to rot. Similarly, Sphagnum burns with too high nutrient load and slows down in growth once it reaches a certain level of saltiness.


One thing I've learned over the years is the importance of using sufficient "starts" to establish new trays. These starts need to be free of weeds and other types of moss: if you start with dirty material, it becomes an uphill battle to clean it up later on.

The amount of light that the sphagnum gets during growth affects the quality of the harvest. full sun creates thicker strands that take longer to break down, whereas shade grown sphagnum produces thinner strands that decompose much quicker. In my climate, it's too hot to grow sphagnum in full sun all year round, but by the coast, I bet you could produce really great quality moss because you can keep them in full sun all the time.

To produce starts, I literally chop (with scissors) the top 1-2" of only the best looking growth points. After that, I harvest the rest, dry all that stuff out. I re-use the soil and trays, no disease or weed issues! Interestingly, I have soil in the tray that is approaching maybe 8 years in age and it's still good! The medium is recycled, old spahgnum moss that was from my disa plants that perished years ago!

Poor growing sphagnum is difficult to use as starting material, so be sure to harvest "starts" only when your sphagnum matts are as happy as can be. You want to cover the new tray with a generous layer of healthy, green growth. A single full grown tray can produce a generous amount of "seed" sufficient enough to start 4 trays. What I've learned is if things slow down in the beginning or it takes a long time to see new growth, or your spaghnum crashes during growth, that can cause a year or more delay! In other words, it'll take 2 years instead of 1 year to produce the same amount of sphagnum.

Here's the next batch of sphagnum, planted only a few days ago. Look at how healthy and happy it looks, I might be tricking myself but it seems like this stuff has already started growing. I'm giving it morning sun and afternoon shade for now, but as it continues to cool, these will slowly be placed in full sun for the winter.



growing a few more trays this year:





A different species that I suspect is native to Georgia, but I'm not sure. Will this species or variety be as productive and good quality as the other strain I'm growing? No clue, but I'll grow them side by side and compare results:

posts.body_html:
It gets over 100F here in Northern California pretty much every late summer/early fall. I have to move my trays around depending on the weather: right now, they're in full sun when the highs are 60-75F, humidity is probably between 30-60%, but that seems to be irrelevant because the plants are watered every day and create their own microclimate.

During the summer, my sphagnum gets morning sun and pure shade all afternoon long. Ideally, if you have cool nights during the summer, you might be able to get away with building a shade structure with 75% shade cloth (only 25% of the light passes through) in full sun, but even that might get too hot. The balancing act is to keep the plant cool yet with as much direct sunlight as possible.

posts.body_html:
There are different forms of Sphagnum.
My form is a very robust one.
If watered from the top it is growing like hell.
My whole bog is full of that (suppressing unwanted plants very successfully).
I plant Heliamphora, some Utricularia, Nepenthes, some Drosera into living Sphagnum.
In the pots of Sarracenia and Cephalotus I add some Sphagnum. If the Sphagnum stops to grow it is indicating that I have to change the soil.

BT

Oct 30, 2018 13:19:47 GMT -5 meizzwang said:
It gets over 100F here in Northern California pretty much every late summer/early fall. I have to move my trays around depending on the weather: right now, they're in full sun when the highs are 60-75F, humidity is probably between 30-60%, but that seems to be irrelevant because the plants are watered every day and create their own microclimate.

During the summer, my sphagnum gets morning sun and pure shade all afternoon long. Ideally, if you have cool nights during the summer, you might be able to get away with building a shade structure with 75% shade cloth (only 25% of the light passes through) in full sun, but even that might get too hot. The balancing act is to keep the plant cool yet with as much direct sunlight as possible.

Well, I guess that means I should keep growing it inside for now It’s good to hear it can take some heat, though. I do wonder about the duration: we certainly don’t have cool summer nights — mid to upper 70s is typical at night from May until September. And our days are hot, too. Most of the summer is 95°+ (with quite a few 100°+ days), and virtually my all of it is 90°+ unless something unusual happens.

Once I’ve got more sphagnum, I might try some outside, but I ain’t all that optimistic. My outdoor carnivores don’t even grow any star moss, much less sphagnum.

There are a handful of sphagnum bogs near-ish (~50-100 mi) to me, but they’re all on top of springs — our groundwater is ~70°. All of the sphagnum I’ve seen growing in Texas was in pretty shady spots — while I don’t know about the bogs near me, at least in Southeast TX, the open areas have no sphagnum at all.

beautytubes — that’s interesting to hear that the strains vary a lot in strength and tolerance. I’d thought they were all pretty similar.

The other thing I’d be worried about is watering frequency — I mean, I stopped growing flytraps in LFS because it dried so fast, and I imagine live sphagnum would be similar. Even once I get an ro filter for my hose, that’s still lots of water. And summer drought isn’t unusual at all — while it’s usually not bad enough to make them restrict hose watering, that isn’t unheard of (it’s happened once or twice in my life).

In Europe we know about 40 (!) different Sphagnum species. Some of them are close to extinction in Austria / Germany because of eutrophication (nutrients from the agriculture transferred by the wind into our last surviving bogs) and (fake!) climate change.


I took plenty of different Sphagnum species from other cultivators. One of these species is very aggressive and tolerates nearly every culture method and temperature range, except wrong water and low light conditions. It is a species growing in the bogs around my location here. That’s why I planted it also into my bog. Hence I have always enough Sphagnum available for my cultures.


PLEASE DO NOT PLANT OUT UNKNOWN SPHAGNUM SPECIES EVEN INTO YOUR OWN OUTDOOR BOGS: it might be very invasive and it could destroy your natural habitats very fast!


BT

PLEASE DO NOT PLANT OUT UNKNOWN SPHAGNUM SPECIES EVEN INTO YOUR OWN OUTDOOR BOGS: it might be very invasive and it could destroy your natural habitats very fast!
BT
